concepts.definition: The low PWM range in which the motor does not turn because it cannot overcome friction. On the robot in the simulation it is about 51 and below.
concepts.example: At PWM 40 the motor hums but the wheel does not move.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking 128 is half speed; the speed is proportional not to the PWM but to the difference PWM − dead zone.

concepts.definition: The highest speed the wheel reaches at PWM 255; 0.396 m/s on the robot in the lessons.
concepts.example: From the measured slope: 0.194 cm/s × (255 − 51), about 39.6 cm/s.
concepts.pitfall: Using V_MAX with the value from another robot or from a flat battery.

concepts.definition: Drawing a straight line through two points that can be measured well to find the slope, the end of the dead zone and the maximum speed.
concepts.example: If you measure 9.4 cm/s at PWM 100 and 28.8 cm/s at PWM 200, the speed crosses zero at about PWM 51.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking the first PWM you notice by eye (57) is the end of the dead zone; the real end is where the speed line crosses zero.

concepts.definition: The function that turns the requested speed into PWM: PWM = OLU_PWM + (255 − OLU_PWM) · v / V_MAX. For very small requests it returns 0.
concepts.example: When you ask for 20 cm/s, the function gives 154; the robot really goes at about 20 cm/s.
concepts.pitfall: Forgetting the dead zone and writing PWM = 255 · v / V_MAX; at slow speeds the PWM stays inside the dead zone.

concepts.definition: Measuring OLU_PWM and V_MAX again when the battery, floor, wheels or motor change.
concepts.example: When you move from carpet to a wooden floor, the dead zone changes; you measure the numbers again.
concepts.pitfall: Calibrating with a flat battery and driving with a full one; the speeds do not match.

quiz.prompt:
Calibration: OLU_PWM = 51, V_MAX = 0.396 m/s. What does hizdanPwm(0.25) return (for 0.25 m/s, with rounding)?

Formula: 51 + (int)(204 * v / V_MAX + 0.5)
quiz.explanation: 204 · 0.25 / 0.396 is about 128.8; with +0.5 it is 129.3, and cut to an int it becomes 129. 51 + 129 = 180. Forgetting to add the dead zone (51) gives 129; that value is a speed far below 0.25 m/s.

quiz.prompt: On a robot, 10 cm/s was measured at PWM 100 and 30 cm/s at PWM 200. If the speed rises linearly, what is the end of the dead zone (the PWM where the speed is zero)?
quiz.explanation: Slope = (30 − 10) / (200 − 100) = 0.2 cm/s per PWM unit. Zero point = 100 − 10 / 0.2 = 50. You need to look for where the line crosses the PWM axis; taking measurement points such as 10 or 100 as the answer is wrong.

0.003 m/s is below 0.005, so the function returns 0 (so the robot does not wander around just above the dead zone, too slowly to measure). 0.5 m/s is limited to the maximum speed (0.396) and becomes 51 + 204 = 255. 303 would come out without the limit and would overflow analogWrite.

options: The return line: the dead zone is not added, so for 5 cm/s the PWM is 32 and stays inside the dead zone
int should be used instead of float
quiz.explanation: 255 · 0.05 / 0.396 is about 32, which is below 51, so the motor does not turn. The correct mapping starts above the dead zone, in the form 51 + 204 · v / V_MAX. The other options are not the cause of the bug.

quiz.prompt: The robot was calibrated with a full battery. A week later the battery is half empty. How does the robot behave when it asks for 20 cm/s?
options: It still goes at exactly 20 cm/s; calibration is permanent
It does not move at all
It goes slower, because the maximum speed drops as the battery runs down
quiz.explanation: As the battery runs down, the voltage going to the motors drops and the speed is lower at the same PWM; a mapping made with a fixed V_MAX no longer fits. That is why calibration is done with a full battery and repeated from time to time.
